claims.claim: Key-writing rule: 'Write without assumption of perspective' about entry point; use compass directions ('east wall'), never relative ones ('far side').
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: keep descriptions 'short and punchy', don't tell players what to feel, use east/west not left/right, and let the map carry redundant door descriptions.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)

claims.claim: Readers summarizing Lynch's standards: don't provide conclusions, avoid 'if/then' constructs as padding, and don't address the party directly in read-aloud.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)

claims.claim: Robin D. Laws: in hypothetical RPG text drop 'will' — 'If the agents reach the safe house, Keletny burns the car'; also avoid passive voice and 'to be' + verb pairs.
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)

claims.claim: Ray Vallese's editor's guide devotes a section to 'using present tense instead of future tense' and to 'avoiding rampant capitalization' — two habits of RPG manuscripts an editor corrects.
claims.source: Ray Vallese — Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers (book page)
claims.quote: using present tense instead of future tense

claims.feature: describe what can be sensed, not what can't
claims.claim: Merwin's epistemic rule: 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot' — no crate contents, but never omit the 50-foot chasm.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot

claims.claim: Words like 'seems' and 'appears' telegraph tricks: 'If something "appears to be" to the characters, it "is"' — let Perception checks, not hedges, create the distinction.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: If something 'appears to be' to the characters, it 'is'

claims.claim: Include only environmental details PCs will interact with; the smell of flowers can go 'unless you happen to be DMing for a party comprised solely of elves or florists'.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: a party comprised solely of elves or florists

claims.claim: 'Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge': no evil soliloquies, no coronation cutscenes; keep passages short and let PCs act.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)

claims.claim: 'Read your boxed text aloud to check readability' — tongue-twisters, unintended alliteration and odd phrasing are invisible on the page.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

claims.claim: Lynch's most-cited rule as summarized: replace the abstract judgment ('a cruel bully') with the concrete action ('Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll'); aim for 'the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait'; specificity, not mere detail.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)
claims.quote: the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait

claims.claim: tenfootpole grades language on a four-point scale topped by 'Succinct and evocative', lists 'Terse writing style' and 'Evocative atmosphere' as requirements, and states 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing'.
Lynch praises one 5e read-aloud for avoiding 'the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud' and for capturing a social scene in progress.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)
claims.quote: the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud

claims.claim: Skerples: use find-and-replace to hunt filler words ('little, big, grand, tall, dark') and swap in evocative choices; 'Every sentence needs to fight for its life in a dungeon key.'
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Every sentence needs to fight for its life

claims.claim: Gus L.: not 'evil idol' but 'toothy glare' or 'sharp edged obsidian'; include non-visual senses but never room history, future or emotions.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)

verdicts.trueWording: Rule 8: Write without assumption of perspective.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim as the Rule 8 heading. Compass limb also verbatim: 'When I do describe a door, I describe it as being on the east or north wall, not the far or right one.' Byline 'Misha F', Tuesday, April 28, 2026, confirmed. Author's own retrospective adds that the GM will likely strip the directional information out again.

verdicts.trueWording: Keep the descriptions short and punchy.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), title 'Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions | Designing Dungeons'. All four limbs found: quote verbatim; section heading 'Don't tell the players what to feel'; 'Writing down terms like "the door to the right" will become confusing... Instead, use cardinal directions'; and under 'Let the map work for you' — 'If something appears on the map, you don't have to waste space describing it... you can avoid repetitive descriptions of all the doors in a room.' The bylines Josh McCrowell / Warren D do not appear on this chapter page itself (site-level attribution, not a claim limb).

verdicts.trueWording: Don't give conclusions; don't use if/then; don't address the party
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Claim carries no quote, so no verbatim test applies; the substance is supported almost word for word by the comment of 'noisician', December 30, 2022 (matches the stated page field), offering '3 pieces of Bryce Advice': 'Don't give conclusions, just describe and let the players come to their own conclusions'; 'Don't use "if/then" constructs. I think this is mainly because it tends to be filler... "if/then" phrasing could be used to pad almost anything, but shouldn't'; 'Don't address the party directly in read-aloud, this typically takes decision making away from the players.' The framing 'Readers summarizing Lynch's standards' is exact — these are a commenter's additions, not the post body.

verdicts.trueWording: If the agents reach the safe house, Keletny burns the car.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), 'Five Keys to Punchier Prose', 'By Robin D. Laws'. Quote verbatim in the corrected example under the section heading 'Deprecation of the "will"' ('In this construction, "will" is totally unnecessary'). Passive-voice limb verbatim: 'Avoid the passive voice'. The 'to be' + verb limb verbatim: 'look for instances of the verb "to be"... Most sentences pair these with an additional verb... reconfigure to drop the "to be"'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'devotes a section to' — the page lists both only as topics the guide covers, never as sections
verdicts.trueWording: It covers such topics as avoiding rampant capitalization, present tense
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Both quoted phrases appear verbatim inside a single sentence: 'It covers such topics as using gender-neutral language, ... avoiding rampant capitalization, ... using present tense instead of future tense, changing passive voice to active voice...'. The page is the book's marketing page for 'Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers' (45 pages, by Ray Vallese, 20+ years editing games), so the editor-corrects-RPG-manuscripts limb holds. Nothing on the page states either topic gets its own section; the only mention of sections is inside a reader review ('Each section gives solid advice'). No table of contents is published on this page.

verdicts.trueWording: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), 'Thinking Outside the Boxed Text', August 27, 2010 by Shawn Merwin. Quote verbatim as the heading of Tip 3. Both illustrative limbs are the page's own: the omission failure is 'the 50-foot-wide chasm between the doorway and the altar', and the over-telling failure is boxed text describing 'large crates full of mining equipment' when 'The characters couldn't know that without opening them'.

verdicts.trueWording: If something 'appears to be' to the characters, it 'is' to the characters.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), same essay. Quote verbatim; the claim's quote truncates the sentence, which on the page ends '...it "is" to the characters.' Heading is 'Tip 4. Avoid "seems to be" or "appears to be."' Telegraphing limb verbatim: 'Those words generally mean that some trick or diversion is in the offing.' Perception limb verbatim: 'Let those Perception or Spot checks separate the "seems" from the "is."'

verdicts.trueWording: unless you happen to be DMing for a party comprised solely of elves or florists
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), same essay. Quote verbatim, and the full sentence is the claim's second limb: 'The smell of flowers in the sunny glade can probably be left out, unless you happen to be DMing for a party comprised solely of elves or florists.' Relevance limb verbatim in the preceding sentence: 'leave in only the details about the environment that the PCs need to know about because they will have to interact with them.'

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), same essay. Quote verbatim as the Tip 2 heading, with 'There are three main kinds of problem with this novelist's urge'. Soliloquy limb: subhead '2b. The villain's soliloquy' plus 'instead of having the evil guy do the soliloquy, let him talk with the characters interactively'. Coronation limb verbatim: 'The characters just saved the prince, and now they get to watch his coronation.' Short-and-act limb verbatim: 'find a way to keep the passages short, and give the PCs the chance to interact with the scene in some way.'

verdicts.trueWording: Tip 5. Read your boxed text aloud to check readability
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text' by Shawn Merwin, Nov 6, 2019 — the article body rendered server-side, no summarizer used. Quote verbatim as the Tip 5 heading. Second limb verbatim: 'Trouble areas like tongue-twisters, funny-sounding phrases, unintended alliteration, and other pitfalls are hard to spot on the page but easy to hear when spoken.'

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'Lynch's most-cited rule' — the page nowhere ranks this rule's prominence or citation frequency
verdicts.trueWording: Go for the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in item 21 of Jon Miller's summary, followed by the exact example the claim gives: 'Instead of stating "One of the guards in the camp is a cruel bully," say "The burly Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll, and then snatches Tobias's roasted chicken from his hand and quickly gobbles it down."' The 'specificity, not mere detail' limb IS on the page but NOT in the post the claim cites — it is a 2021 comment by 'Clever Munkey' ('Try for specificity not simply detail'), which Jon Miller endorses in reply ('Specific but not verbose'). The superlative 'most-cited' is the researcher's own framing, unverifiable from this page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'as requirements', and the four-point Language scale is not Bryce Lynch's — it belongs to a second reviewer, 'The Pretty Girl'
verdicts.trueWording: What I'm looking for in an adventure module; Language 4 - Succinct and evocative
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Third limb verbatim: 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing.' Both phrases verbatim as standalone bullets: 'Evocative atmosphere.' and 'Terse writing style'. But Bryce's list is prefaced 'What I'm looking for in an adventure module may not be what you are looking for. I try to avoid giving a module a rating' — and the same list explicitly grades requirement status elsewhere ('Wandering monster tables are generally required'; an overland portion is 'nice, but not required'), so neither of these two is labelled a requirement. Separately, the Language rubric (4 - Succinct and evocative / 2 - Conversational but clear / 1 - You should have hired an English Major to edit this / 0 - Very wordy/incomprehensible) sits in a later section headed 'The Pretty Girl', a second reviewer who introduces herself as 'not the gourmand that Bryce is' and calls it 'My ratings system'. It is on tenfootpole's standards page, so 'tenfootpole grades' holds, but the claim's source attribution to Bryce Lynch does not. Note also the rubric spans 0-4 with four defined rungs (no 3), so 'four-point scale' is loose.

verdicts.trueWording: it's not the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), '(5e) Death in the Wood', Posted on February 9, 2019 by Bryce Lynch. Quote verbatim (including the misspelling 'drivil'). Praise limb: 'It's also pretty well written, which I don't think I've said more than three or four times?' Social-scene limb verbatim: 'The read-aloud tends to be describing a social interaction though, as if you just walked up on something happening... It does a good job of communicating the social vibe going on.' The praise is qualified in the same breath — 'It's still too long and the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones' — which the claim does not assert either way.

verdicts.trueWording: Every sentence needs to fight for its life in a dungeon key.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), 'OSR: Sharpening the Axe - How I Plan and Write RPG Books', dated 2019/09/05, Skerples. Quote verbatim, and the page continues 'Evoke. Make it visceral. Make it real.' Filler limb verbatim and with the claim's exact word list: 'Use find and replace to locate common "filler" words: little, big, grand, tall, dark, etc. Everyone has their own bugbears. Replace with evocative choices.'

verdicts.trueWording: An idol shouldn't be described as 'evil'... rather it has a 'toothy glare' or is 'sharp edged obsidian'
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), 'Dungeon Design, Process and Keys', Monday, December 19, 2022, Gus L. Quote verbatim under 'a. Don't generalize: Describe specifics'; the page's negative example is 'evil' or 'forbidding' for an idol, matching the claim's 'evil idol'. Senses limb: 'there is advice to remember that senses other than sight exist: smells, sounds, and sensation etc.'  followed by 'This old advice to include other senses is still good' (with a caution against including everything). History/future limbs verbatim as headings under '7) Limit Your Description To The Room As It Is!': 'a. Don't describe the room's past.' and 'b. Don't describe the room's future.' Emotions limb is tip 10: 'Don't Tell the Characters How to Feel!' — 'You don't get to tell the players how their characters feel emotionally (barring creepy magic) or even physically.'
